```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(1)
```

## Problem 1

```{r}
shared_birthday = function(group_size) {
  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = group_size, replace = TRUE)
  any(duplicated(birthdays))
}

birthday_results = expand_grid(
  group_size = 2:50,
  iteration = 1:10000
) |>
  mutate(shared = map_lgl(group_size, shared_birthday)) |>
  group_by(group_size) |>
  summarise(probability = mean(shared), .groups = "drop")

birthday_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = probability)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    x = "Number of people",
    y = "Probability of a shared birthday"
  )
```

The probability of a shared birthday increases as the group gets larger.
It is about one-half with 23 people and close to one with 50 people.
Larger groups have more pairs of people who could share a birthday.

## Problem 2

```{r}
study_data = tibble(
  file_name = list.files("data", pattern = "\\.csv$")
) |>
  mutate(
    observations = map(
      str_c("data/", file_name),
      read_csv,
      show_col_types = FALSE
    ),
    file_name = str_remove(file_name, "\\.csv$")
  ) |>
  separate(file_name, into = c("arm", "subject_id"), sep = "_") |>
  unnest(observations) |>
  pivot_longer(
    starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "week_",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    week = as.integer(week),
    arm = recode(arm, con = "Control", exp = "Experimental")
  )

study_data |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = week,
    y = observation,
    group = interaction(arm, subject_id),
    color = arm
  )) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ arm) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Observation", color = "Study arm")
```

The experimental group generally increases over time, while the control
group fluctuates without a clear upward trend. By the later weeks,
observations in the experimental group are generally higher. Individual
participants vary within both groups.

## Problem 3

```{r}
sim_t_test = function(mu) {
  sample_values = rnorm(30, mean = mu, sd = 5)

  t.test(sample_values, mu = 0) |>
    broom::tidy() |>
    select(mu_hat = estimate, p_value = p.value)
}

test_results = expand_grid(
  true_mu = 0:6,
  iteration = 1:5000
) |>
  mutate(result = map(true_mu, sim_t_test)) |>
  unnest(result)

test_summary = test_results |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarise(
    rejection_rate = mean(p_value < 0.05),
    mean_estimate = mean(mu_hat),
    mean_rejected = mean(mu_hat[p_value < 0.05]),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

test_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = rejection_rate)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  labs(
    x = "True mean",
    y = "Proportion of tests rejecting the null"
  )
```

As the true mean moves farther from zero, power increases and approaches
one. Larger effects are easier to distinguish from random variation when
the sample size and standard deviation stay fixed. At a true mean of
zero, the rejection rate is about 0.05; this is the false-positive rate,
not power against a false null hypothesis.

```{r}
test_summary |>
  select(true_mu, mean_estimate, mean_rejected) |>
  pivot_longer(
    mean_estimate:mean_rejected,
    names_to = "samples",
    values_to = "average_estimate"
  ) |>
  mutate(samples = recode(
    samples,
    mean_estimate = "All samples",
    mean_rejected = "Rejected tests only"
  )) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = average_estimate, color = samples)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  labs(x = "True mean", y = "Average estimated mean", color = "Samples")
```

Across all samples, the average estimated mean is close to the true mean.
Among rejected tests, estimates tend to be too high for small positive
true means because samples with larger estimated effects are more likely
to be significant. This difference decreases as power increases and most
tests are rejected. At a true mean of zero, the two-sided test selects
both positive and negative extremes, so their average remains near zero
in expectation, with some simulation variation.
